did_you_know.text: The vision begins with the angel awakening Zechariah, described as someone waking from sleep. This emphasizes the transition into a state of seeing a vision.
The lampstand Zechariah sees is made entirely of gold, with a bowl on top. It has seven lamps, and each lamp has seven channels for conveying oil.
The two olive trees stand on either side of the bowl of the lampstand—one on its right and one on its left. This detail connects the source of the oil with the light of the lampstand.
Zechariah does not understand the meaning of the vision, so he asks the angel twice. When asked whether he knows its meaning, he honestly replies, “No, my lord.”

The message to Zerubbabel emphasizes that success will not be achieved through military might or human strength alone, but through the Spirit of the LORD: “Not by might nor by power, but by my Spirit.”

The great mountain symbolizes an obstacle standing before Zerubbabel, but it will become level ground. Then Zerubbabel will bring out the capstone, and the people will greet it with cries of “Grace, grace to it!”

The verse credits Zerubbabel with both laying the foundation of the temple and completing its construction. In this way, it expresses the promise that the work begun by his hands will also be completed by his hands.

The verse warns against despising the day of small beginnings. The plumb line in Zerubbabel’s hand and the seven eyes represent the continuation of the construction and the LORD’s watchful care over the land.

At the end of the vision, the two olive trees are called “the two sons of oil,” and they are described as standing before the Lord of all the earth. In the context of the chapter, they are associated with the religious and political leadership of the period of the return from exile.
